% ===========================
% Section 2 -- Proof program
% ===========================

\section{Proof program ((demonstrated and explained with example)(full top-level reasoning and train-of-thought)(reader facing walkthrough))}\label{sec:ProofProgram}

Suppose you are given the velocity of the fluid at one point and one instant.
You know how fast it is moving and in which direction.
You still do not know how that motion is changing.
A finite velocity can be followed by a failed response, so the velocity value alone cannot tell us whether the same history remains smooth.

To see the next piece of information, follow one particle of the fluid.
Let \(X(t)\) be its path.
The particle moves with the velocity field:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoParticlePath}
  \dot X(t)=u\bigl(X(t),t\bigr).
\end{equation}
Its carried velocity is \(u(X(t),t)\), and the chain rule gives
\begin{align}
  \frac{d}{dt}u\bigl(X(t),t\bigr)
  &=\partial_tu+\bigl(\dot X\cdot\nabla\bigr)u
  \notag\\
  &=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u
  =:D_tu.
  \label{eq:SectionTwoMaterialDerivative}
\end{align}
Every field on the right-hand side is evaluated at \((X(t),t)\).
The operator \(D_t=\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla\) follows the particle and is called the material derivative.
The momentum equation now says
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoMaterialResponse}
  D_tu=-\nabla p+\nu\Delta u.
\end{equation}
This is the particle's acceleration.
Pressure carries the response of the surrounding incompressible field, viscosity acts on the spatial curvature of the velocity, and transport is already present because the particle is moving through that field.
All three terms describe the response of the same fluid at the same time.

Now suppose the velocity stays finite as an alleged endpoint is approached while \(D_tu\) becomes unbounded.
The velocity reading would still look harmless even though the fluid's acceleration had failed.
So acceleration has to travel with velocity in any account of smoothness.

The same problem appears one level higher.
An acceleration can be finite at one instant while its own rate of change fails.
Following the same particle gives that next response:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoMaterialJerk}
  D_t(D_tu)=D_t^2u.
\end{equation}
This is the material jerk.
If the jerk stays finite, we can ask the same question about the change in the jerk.
Each finite level can be the last finite reading before the next response fails.
That means one smooth history has to carry every finite response produced by the same motion.
The full tower now has a concrete job: it records every level at which that response could stop belonging to the fluid.

A particle path gives the physical meaning of the response.
An estimate has to compare the whole field at common spatial points, so the proof returns to the fixed-point rows already introduced in the VPI law.
Write
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoEulerianRows}
  V_n:=\partial_t^nu,
  \qquad
  P_n:=\partial_t^np.
\end{equation}
These are Eulerian rows because the spatial point is held fixed.
The first row \(V_1=\partial_tu\) is one coordinate of the material acceleration:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoAccelerationCoordinateChange}
  D_tu=V_1+(V_0\cdot\nabla)V_0.
\end{equation}
The transport term supplies the part seen only when the motion is followed.

Differentiating the same pressure-complete equation keeps that transport inside every higher row:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoEulerianRecurrence}
  V_{n+1}
  +\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}(V_k\cdot\nabla)V_{n-k}
  +\nabla P_n
  =\nu\Delta V_n,
  \qquad
  \nabla\cdot V_n=0.
\end{equation}
At \(n=0\), this is the original acceleration law written in fixed-point coordinates.
At \(n=1\), it becomes
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoSecondTemporalRow}
  V_2
  +(V_1\cdot\nabla)V_0
  +(V_0\cdot\nabla)V_1
  +\nabla P_1
  =\nu\Delta V_1.
\end{equation}
The term \((V_1\cdot\nabla)V_0\) changes the velocity doing the carrying.
The term \((V_0\cdot\nabla)V_1\) changes the velocity response being carried through the existing flow.
The pressure derivative still comes from the surrounding field, and viscosity now acts on the spatial curvature of \(V_1\).
The next temporal response has pulled spatial derivatives, pressure, and transport into the same row.

This creates two separate directions in the tower.
The index \(n\) tells us how many times the field has been differentiated in time.
The gradients and Laplacian tell us how deeply the same row must be read in space.
One temporal depth does not determine the other spatial depth.
We have to be able to choose both depths independently and still know that their shared entries come from the same fluid.

\divider{Building one finite record}

Start with the spatial direction.
For an integer \(m\geq0\), the Sobolev norm
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoSobolevRow}
  \norm{v}_{H^m(\R^3)}^2
  =
  \sum_{\lvert\alpha\rvert\leq m}
  \norm{\partial_x^\alpha v}_{L^2(\R^3)}^2
\end{equation}
measures every spatial derivative through order \(m\).
It turns one finite part of the pointwise tower into one finite spatial reading.
The space \(L^2(0,T;H^m)\) accumulates that reading over the time interval \((0,T)\).

Now take enough of the tower to watch the velocity, its first Eulerian time response, and the change in that response.
Read \(u\) and \(\partial_tu\) through three spatial derivatives.
Then read \(\partial_tu\) and \(\partial_t^2u\) through one spatial derivative.
The accumulated size of those four entries is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoConcreteRectangle}
\begin{aligned}
  \mathfrak R_{1,2}(u;T)
  ={}&
  \norm{u}_{L^2(0,T;H^3)}^2
  +\norm{\partial_tu}_{L^2(0,T;H^3)}^2
  \\
  &+
  \norm{\partial_tu}_{L^2(0,T;H^1)}^2
  +\norm{\partial_t^2u}_{L^2(0,T;H^1)}^2.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The first line gives the higher spatial reading of the first two temporal rows.
The second line gives the lower spatial reading of their time derivatives.
The same \(\partial_tu\) appears in both lines because it joins the two adjacent temporal blocks.
Its \(H^3\) membership supplies its \(H^1\) membership, so the two blocks overlap on the same derivative.
The material acceleration in this example remains \(\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u\).

Nothing in that construction depends on stopping at temporal depth \(1\) or spatial parameter \(2\).
Choose any finite \(N,M\in\Nzero\).
Reading the first \(N+1\) temporal rows in \(H^{M+1}\), and their time derivatives in \(H^{M-1}\), gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoRectangleNorm}
\begin{aligned}
  \mathfrak R_{N,M}(u;T)
  :={}&
  \sum_{n=0}^{N}
  \norm{\partial_t^n u}_{L^2(0,T;H^{M+1})}^{2}
  \\
  &+
  \sum_{n=0}^{N}
  \norm{\partial_t^{n+1}u}_{L^2(0,T;H^{M-1})}^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For \(M=0\), the lower row is \(H^{-1}\) in the standard inhomogeneous Bessel-potential scale.
This is the adjacent-row rectangle norm.
The one-time-derivative and two-spatial-derivative separation matches the parabolic shape of the VPI recurrence.

The norm measures the velocity rows.
To make those rows one record, we also keep the pressure rows and the differentiated equations that connect them.
For the rapidly decaying whole-space history, pressure is fixed from the same velocity by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoPressureNormalization}
  p=R_iR_j(u_i u_j),
\end{equation}
where \(R_j=\partial_j(-\Delta)^{-1/2}\) is the \(j\)-th Riesz transform.
Call the resulting datum-specific record \(\cR_{N,M}[u_0;T]\).
Every entry in it is a distributional derivative of the history generated by \(u_0\), and every pressure entry uses this same normalization.

Let \([0,T_*)\) be the maximal classical lifespan of that history and suppose the alleged endpoint is finite.
Fix any \(T<T_*\).
The interval \([0,T]\) lies strictly inside the classical lifespan, so for every finite \(n,q\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoStrictClassicalBound}
  \sup_{0\leq t\leq T}
  \norm{\partial_t^n u(t)}_{H^q}
  <\infty.
\end{equation}
Integrating that fixed bound gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoStrictTimeIntegral}
  \norm{\partial_t^n u}_{L^2(0,T;H^q)}^2
  \leq
  T\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}
  \norm{\partial_t^n u(t)}_{H^q}^{2}
  <\infty.
\end{equation}
So every finite rectangle exists on every strict subinterval:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoStrictRectangle}
  \mathfrak R_{N,M}(u;T)<\infty
  \qquad
  \text{for every finite }N,M
  \text{ and every }0<T<T_*.
\end{equation}
The order of that sentence matters.
We choose \(T\) first and then obtain the bound.
As \(T\) moves toward \(T_*\), the bound for one fixed rectangle may still grow without limit.

Before moving the interval, compare two rectangles on the same strict time.
The record \(\cR_{2,3}[u_0;T]\) contains \(u,\partial_tu,\partial_t^2u\) in \(H^4\), together with \(\partial_tu,\partial_t^2u,\partial_t^3u\) in \(H^2\).
Forget the highest temporal entries and use the embeddings \(H^4\hookrightarrow H^3\) and \(H^2\hookrightarrow H^1\).
The four entries left are exactly the entries of \(\cR_{1,2}[u_0;T]\).
The surviving \(u\) and \(\partial_tu\) are the same derivatives that appeared in the larger record.

The same operation works at every finite depth.
If \(N'\leq N\), \(M'\leq M\), and \(T'\leq T\), the restriction map
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoRestrictionMap}
  \rho_{N',M';T'}^{N,M;T}:
  \cR_{N,M}[u_0;T]
  \longrightarrow
  \cR_{N',M'}[u_0;T']
\end{equation}
forgets the higher temporal rows, lowers the spatial order, and shortens the time interval.
The shared velocity and pressure coordinates stay unchanged.
Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoRestrictionCompatibility}
  \rho_{N',M';T'}^{N,M;T}
  \cR_{N,M}[u_0;T]
  =
  \cR_{N',M'}[u_0;T'].
\end{equation}
This is compatibility.
Every larger view returns the same smaller view because both came from the same history.

For a fixed strict time \(T<T_*\), all of these compatible rectangles form the inverse-limit object
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoProjectiveIntersection}
  \cI[u_0;T]
  :=
  \varprojlim_{N,M}\cR_{N,M}[u_0;T].
\end{equation}
The projective intersection keeps one value for every finite temporal and spatial coordinate.
Every lower view is recovered from every higher view by restriction, and the same \(u\) realizes every projection.

This intersection is coordinatewise.
It does not require the infinite sum
\(\sum_{N,M}\mathfrak R_{N,M}(u;T)\)
to be finite.
It also allows one finite pair \((N,M)\) to have a different bound from another pair.
We select a finite coordinate, keep its own finite bound, and require that coordinate to agree everywhere else it appears.

\divider{Moving the record to the terminal time}

For every strict \(T<T_*\), classicality has now supplied the full compatible family.
The possible failure is hiding in what happens while \(T\) approaches the alleged endpoint.
What we know so far is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoStrictQuantifiers}
  \forall\,0<T<T_*,
  \quad
  \forall\,N,M\in\Nzero,
  \qquad
  \mathfrak R_{N,M}(u;T)<\infty.
\end{equation}
Each interval has every finite rectangle.
The statement still permits one fixed rectangle to grow along a sequence \(T_j\uparrow T_*\).

To remove that escape, choose the finite depths first.
The datum and viscosity must then supply one bound that works for every \(T<T_*\).
The exact requirement is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:SectionTwoWholeTerminalQuestion}
  \sup_{0<T<T_*}
  \mathfrak R_{N,M}(u;T)
  \leq
  C_{N,M}(u_0,\nu,T_*)
  <\infty
  \qquad
  \text{for every finite }N,M.
\end{equation}
The constant may depend on the selected temporal and spatial depths.
Its uniformity is only across the expanding time interval.

If this bound fails, some fixed finite rectangle escapes as the endpoint is approached even though every earlier truncation is smooth.
If it holds for every finite pair, every coordinate reaches the whole interval and compatibility keeps the complete family inside one pressure-complete history.
The possible singularity has been forced into one exact place: the loss of a fixed finite rectangle at the terminal face.
The proof burden is now equally exact: after any finite rectangle is chosen, the datum and viscosity must keep that same rectangle bounded all the way to the alleged endpoint.
